A screening mammogram in U.S. community practice — digital breast tomosynthesis, the "3D mammogram" now in routine use — has about 87% sensitivity and 92% specificity ([Lee et al., 2023](#references)): if you have cancer, it comes back positive 87% of the time; if you don't, it comes back negative 92% of the time. About 7 in 1,000 women screened actually have breast cancer. You test positive. What are the odds you have it?

Each dot below is one of 1,000 people screened, red for those who have the condition, dark for those who don't. Drag the sliders to change the numbers; the closing section works through the real ones.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// VM is the shared utility library, loaded globally via _includes/head-scripts.html (js/**). This page uses VM.ui.renderTable and VM.sampling.seededRandom.
VM = window.VM
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// This page draws its grids as inline SVG, not Plotly, so it gets none of
// the automatic re-theming the fullscreen-button patch gives every
// .js-plotly-plot. Depending on vmTheme is what makes it re-theme anyway:
// the generator emits on each toggle, so chartColors recomputes and every
// grid-drawing cell downstream redraws with the new palette. See
// VM.plotting.onThemeChange for why it fires a couple of frames after the
// toggle rather than inline.
vmTheme = Generators.observe(notify => VM.plotting.onThemeChange(notify))

chartColors = VM.plotting.colors(vmTheme)

config = ({
  colors: {
    infected: chartColors.alt,
    healthy: chartColors.ink
  },
  grid: {
    // 1,000 people, not 6,000 dots: at the real 0.7% prevalence the seven
    // people who have the condition have to be seven individually visible
    // marks, which they can't be as 0.7% of a 720px-wide point cloud. This
    // is why natural-frequency pictures (Gigerenzer) are "per 1,000" --
    // small enough for the rarest group to be a countable handful, large
    // enough to hold a 0.7% prevalence at all.
    population: 1000,
    columns: 50,
    // The SVG's coordinate width; it scales to the column's full width via
    // CSS, so this only sets the aspect ratio and the dot size relative to it.
    width: 720,
    // A negative result is drawn as a faded hollow ring, so the solid
    // positives -- the people the page is about -- stand out from a crowd
    // of 900-odd cleared ones instead of competing with it. Full-strength
    // rings read as a second, equally busy pattern on top of the first.
    // Each further test fades the already-cleared people by this factor
    // again (see fadeOpacity), so the picture layers: still solid, cleared
    // by the latest test, cleared before that.
    negativeOpacity: 0.3
  }
})
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// shuffleKeys: one fixed random number per person, generated once at load.
// The shuffled layout places people in order of this key, so a person keeps
// the same slot as the sliders move -- raising prevalence adds red dots
// without reshuffling the ones already there -- and a subset (everyone who
// tested positive) keeps its members' relative positions. Seeded for the
// same reason every other page on the site seeds its RNG: a shared URL
// should reproduce the picture it was shared from.
shuffleKeys = {
  const random = VM.sampling.seededRandom(20260801)
  const keys = []
  for (let i = 0; i < config.grid.population; i++) keys.push(random())
  return keys
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// splitByTest: the four outcomes as whole people, given how many of the
// group have the condition and how many don't. Rounded at each split -- a
// grid draws people, not fractions -- so the counts always sum exactly.
function splitByTest(infected, healthy, sensitivity, specificity) {
  const truePositives = Math.round(infected * sensitivity)
  const falseNegatives = infected - truePositives
  const falsePositives = Math.round(healthy * (1 - specificity))
  const trueNegatives = healthy - falsePositives
  return {
    infected, healthy, truePositives, falseNegatives, falsePositives, trueNegatives,
    positives: truePositives + falsePositives,
    negatives: falseNegatives + trueNegatives
  }
}

// ppvOf/npvOf: the exact values, from the probabilities rather than from
// the rounded counts in the picture. Those are the products Bayes' theorem
// multiplies -- P(positive and infected) = prevalence x sensitivity, and so
// on -- whereas "6 of 85" is those products rounded to whole people, and
// can differ from the exact value by a rounding (at 0.6% prevalence, the
// old 2D-mammography default, the picture gave 5/114 = 4.4% against an
// exact 4.6%); the closing section quotes the exact one.
function ppvOf(prevalence, sensitivity, specificity) {
  const truePositive = prevalence * sensitivity
  const falsePositive = (1 - prevalence) * (1 - specificity)
  return truePositive / (truePositive + falsePositive)
}

function npvOf(prevalence, sensitivity, specificity) {
  const trueNegative = (1 - prevalence) * specificity
  const falseNegative = prevalence * (1 - sensitivity)
  return trueNegative / (trueNegative + falseNegative)
}

// formatPct: PPV/NPV are 0/0 when a group is empty (e.g. prevalence or
// sensitivity dragged to an extreme) -- guard against rendering "NaN%".
function formatPct(value) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(value)) return "—"
  return (value * 100).toFixed(1) + "%"
}

// paramNumber: reads a URL query parameter as a number for a slider's
// initial value, falling back to `fallback` when the parameter is absent
// or not a valid number (e.g. a hand-edited or stale link).
function paramNumber(params, key, fallback) {
  const raw = params.get(key)
  if (raw === null) return fallback
  const parsed = Number(raw)
  if (!Number.isFinite(parsed)) return fallback
  return parsed
}

// makePeople: one record per person, in category order -- everyone with
// the condition first (caught cases, then missed ones), then everyone
// without (false alarms, then correct negatives). `keys[i]` is person i's
// fixed shuffle key. `clearedRound` is the test that returned this
// person's first negative result -- 1 here, for the first test -- or null
// while they are still testing positive; applyRetest fills in round 2.
function makePeople(split, keys) {
  const people = []
  const add = (count, infected, clearedRound) => {
    for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
      people.push({infected, clearedRound, key: keys[people.length]})
    }
  }
  add(split.truePositives, true, null)
  add(split.falseNegatives, true, 1)
  add(split.falsePositives, false, null)
  add(split.trueNegatives, false, 1)
  return people
}

// applyRetest: gives everyone still positive after round `round - 1` their
// result from test `round`, in place. The same people stay in the same
// slots -- nobody is re-laid out -- and among each group (the true
// positives, the false positives) the first `split.truePositives` /
// `split.falsePositives` of them in category order stay positive; the
// rest are cleared in this round.
function applyRetest(people, split, round) {
  let infectedKept = 0
  let healthyKept = 0
  for (const person of people) {
    if (person.clearedRound !== null) continue
    if (person.infected) {
      infectedKept++
      if (infectedKept > split.truePositives) person.clearedRound = round
    } else {
      healthyKept++
      if (healthyKept > split.falsePositives) person.clearedRound = round
    }
  }
  return people
}

// fadeOpacity: how faded a person cleared in `clearedRound` is drawn after
// `rounds` tests -- one step of negativeOpacity per test since they were
// cleared, so the latest test's negatives are the most visible rings and
// earlier ones recede behind them. A missed case (`infected` and cleared)
// never fades: the fade is there to push the crowd of correctly cleared
// people into the background, and the one the test got wrong is exactly
// the dot the reader should still be able to find.
function fadeOpacity(rounds, clearedRound, infected) {
  if (infected) return 1
  return Math.pow(config.grid.negativeOpacity, rounds - clearedRound + 1)
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// drawGrid: one dot per person, laid out column-major on a grid. Hue is the
// person's true condition; a solid dot is still testing positive, a hollow
// one has been cleared, faded by how many tests ago (fadeOpacity).
// options.rounds is how many tests have been applied: 0 draws the bare
// population with every dot solid -- the test is what hollows out the
// people it clears, so whoever is still solid afterwards is a positive
// result. Every grid on the page draws the same people in the same slots,
// so the reader can follow one dot from picture to picture.
//
// Returns an inline SVG with a viewBox, stretched to the column's full
// width by CSS -- so the grid is always page-wide, whatever the column
// width, rather than a fixed 720px block sitting left-aligned in it.
function drawGrid(people, options = {}) {
  const rounds = options.rounds ?? 1
  const width = config.grid.width
  const count = people.length
  const columns = config.grid.columns
  const rows = Math.ceil(count / columns)
  const pitch = width / columns
  const height = rows * pitch
  const radius = pitch * 0.36
  const ringWidth = Math.max(1.2, radius * 0.28)

  // Slot order: by fixed shuffle key, or by category (the order people
  // arrive in from makePeople).
  const order = []
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) order.push(i)
  if (layout === "shuffled") {
    order.sort((a, b) => people[a].key - people[b].key)
  }

  let circles = ""
  for (let slot = 0; slot < count; slot++) {
    const person = people[order[slot]]
    const cx = (Math.floor(slot / rows) + 0.5) * pitch
    const cy = ((slot % rows) + 0.5) * pitch
    let color = config.colors.healthy
    if (person.infected) color = config.colors.infected
    if (rounds > 0 && person.clearedRound !== null && person.clearedRound <= rounds) {
      const opacity = fadeOpacity(rounds, person.clearedRound, person.infected)
      circles += `<circle cx="${cx.toFixed(2)}" cy="${cy.toFixed(2)}" r="${(radius - ringWidth / 2).toFixed(2)}" fill="none" stroke="${color}" stroke-width="${ringWidth.toFixed(2)}" opacity="${opacity.toFixed(3)}"/>`
    } else {
      circles += `<circle cx="${cx.toFixed(2)}" cy="${cy.toFixed(2)}" r="${radius.toFixed(2)}" fill="${color}"/>`
    }
  }

  // Returned inside a <div>, not as the bare <svg>: Quarto's OJS output
  // inspects a bare SVGSVGElement as a value ("SVGSVGElement {}") instead
  // of inserting it, whereas an HTMLElement is inserted as a node.
  const holder = document.createElement("div")
  holder.innerHTML = `<svg viewBox="0 0 ${width} ${height.toFixed(2)}" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img">${circles}</svg>`
  const svg = holder.firstElementChild
  svg.style.display = "block"
  svg.style.width = "100%"
  svg.style.height = "auto"
  return holder
}

// swatch: the inline legend mark used in the explanation panels -- a solid
// dot, or a hollow ring at the given fade -- matching how the grids draw
// people.
function swatch(color, filled, opacity = 1) {
  let cls = "ppv-swatch"
  if (filled) cls += " filled"
  return html`<i class="${cls}" style="color: ${color}; opacity: ${opacity}"></i>`
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// infectedCount: how many of the 1,000 have the condition -- prevalence
// rounded to whole people, so the first grid shows exactly this many red.
infectedCount = Math.round(prevalence * config.grid.population)

// populationPeople: the population before any test, built with a perfect
// test (sensitivity and specificity both 1) so every person's `positive`
// flag is just their condition. That keeps this grid out of the two test
// sliders' reactive graph -- it only redraws when prevalence or the layout
// changes -- and, since the category order (infected first) and the keys
// are the same as `people` below, each dot sits in the same slot in both.
populationPeople = makePeople(splitByTest(infectedCount, config.grid.population - infectedCount, 1, 1), shuffleKeys)
```

```{ojs}
// The population before any test is applied: prevalence alone, every dot
// solid.
drawGrid(populationPeople, {rounds: 0})
```

```{ojs}
html`<div class="ojs-panel"><strong>The population.</strong> Each dot is one of 1,000 people; ${swatch(config.colors.infected, true)} <strong style="color: ${config.colors.infected}">red</strong> are the ${initialSplit.infected} (${formatPct(prevalence)}) who have the condition, ${swatch(config.colors.healthy, true)} dark the ${initialSplit.healthy} who don't. Nobody has been tested yet.</div>`
```

Now apply a test to that population. The two sliders below set how often it is right about each group: sensitivity is the share of the red dots it catches, specificity the share of the dark dots it correctly clears. The test hollows out everyone it clears; whoever is still solid afterwards has a positive result — true positives among the red, false positives among the dark.

```{ojs}
viewof layout = {

  let initial = "shuffled"
  if (params.get("layout") === "sorted") initial = "sorted"
  // Shuffled is the honest default -- in a real population you can't tell

  // category into a block, which is easier to count. Every grid on the

  return Inputs.radio(new Map([["Shuffled", "shuffled"], ["Sorted", "sorted"]]), {value: initial, label: "Layout"})
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// urlSync: mirrors the current control values into the URL's query string
// on every change, so the address bar stays a shareable link. Runs
// directly off the reactive values (no "Plot" commit step, unlike the
// text-expression fields on other pages) since redrawing a thousand
// circles is cheap enough to redo on every drag tick.
urlSync = {
  const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)
  params.set("prevalence", String(prevalence))
  params.set("sensitivity", String(sensitivity))
  params.set("specificity", String(specificity))
  params.set("layout", layout)
  history.replaceState(null, "", `${window.location.pathname}?${params}`)
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// initialSplit: how the 1,000 split by condition, and then by the first
// test. split1: how the first test's positives split under a second test
// -- their split by condition is exact (they *are* the true and false
// positives), so only the second test's outcome is rounded again.
initialSplit = splitByTest(infectedCount, config.grid.population - infectedCount, sensitivity, specificity)
split1 = splitByTest(initialSplit.truePositives, initialSplit.falsePositives, sensitivity, specificity)
// people: every person's result from both tests, in one array -- the
// "after one test" grid draws it with rounds: 1, the retest grid with
// rounds: 2, so the two pictures are the same people in the same slots.
people = applyRetest(makePeople(initialSplit, shuffleKeys), split1, 2)
initialPpv = ppvOf(prevalence, sensitivity, specificity)
initialNpv = npvOf(prevalence, sensitivity, specificity)
```

```{ojs}
drawGrid(people, {rounds: 1})
```

```{ojs}
html`<div class="ojs-panel"><strong>After one test.</strong> A hollow dot is a negative result: ${swatch(config.colors.healthy, false, fadeOpacity(1, 1, false))} the ${initialSplit.trueNegatives} people correctly cleared, faded into the background, and ${swatch(config.colors.infected, false)} the ${initialSplit.falseNegatives} the test missed, left at full strength so you can still find them. The solid dots are everyone who tests positive — ${initialSplit.positives} people, of whom ${swatch(config.colors.infected, true)} ${initialSplit.truePositives} actually have the condition and ${swatch(config.colors.healthy, true)} ${initialSplit.falsePositives} don't. Positive predictive value (chance you have the condition, given a positive test): <strong>${formatPct(initialPpv)}</strong>. Negative predictive value: <strong>${formatPct(initialNpv)}</strong>.</div>`
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// The repeat test is applied to the first test's positives only -- the
// population going in is those ${initialSplit.positives} people, whose
// prevalence is the first round's PPV.
newPrevalence1 = initialPpv
ppv1 = ppvOf(newPrevalence1, sensitivity, specificity)
npv1 = npvOf(newPrevalence1, sensitivity, specificity)
```

```{ojs}

html`<div class="ojs-panel"><strong>After a second test of the positives</strong> — the same 1,000 people in the same places. Only the ${initialSplit.positives} who were solid above are tested again; going in, ${initialSplit.truePositives} of them have the condition, so the effective prevalence is now ${formatPct(newPrevalence1)} rather than ${formatPct(prevalence)}. Everyone the first test cleared fades a step further (${swatch(config.colors.healthy, false, fadeOpacity(2, 1, false))}); the ${split1.negatives} the second test clears become hollow (${swatch(config.colors.healthy, false, fadeOpacity(2, 2, false))} ${split1.trueNegatives} false alarms resolved, ${swatch(config.colors.infected, false)} ${split1.falseNegatives} missed this time — a missed case never fades). ${split1.positives} people are still solid, ${swatch(config.colors.infected, true)} ${split1.truePositives} of them red. PPV jumps to <strong>${formatPct(ppv1)}</strong>.</div>`
```

```{ojs}
summaryTable = {
  const row = (step, effectivePrevalence, split, ppv, npv) => [
    step,
    formatPct(effectivePrevalence),
    `${split.truePositives} of ${split.positives}`,
    formatPct(ppv),
    formatPct(npv)
  ]

  return VM.ui.renderTable({
    html,
    headers: ["Round", "Effective prevalence", "Positives who have it (in the picture)", "PPV", "NPV"],
    filename: "bayes-theorem-summary.csv",
    rows: [
      row("1 positive test", prevalence, initialSplit, initialPpv, initialNpv),
      row("2 positive tests", newPrevalence1, split1, ppv1, npv1)
    ]
  })
}
```

:::

Even with a highly accurate test, a positive result is far less conclusive than it sounds when the condition is rare: there are so many more healthy people that a small false-positive rate among them can outnumber the true positives among the few who are actually sick. That's what the solid dots above show — the positives are a handful of red in a crowd of dark, and at low prevalence the dark ones dominate.

This is also why retesting works so well. Each repeat test is applied to a population where the *effective* prevalence has already jumped to the previous round's PPV, so the same sensitivity and specificity produce a much sharper result — and the chance of missing the condition across repeated tests (the false-negative rate, compounding each round) shrinks just as fast. These updates are exactly what Bayes' theorem formalizes:

$$
P(\text{condition} \mid \text{positive}) = \frac{P(\text{positive} \mid \text{condition})\, P(\text{condition})}{P(\text{positive})}.
$$

## What this means for a real mammogram

At the real prevalence of 0.66% — 5.8 cancers found plus 0.8 missed per 1,000 screens, rounded to 7 in 1,000 as the default above; [reset the sliders](?prevalence=0.007&sensitivity=0.87&specificity=0.92) if you've moved them — the PPV is about 7%: in the picture, 6 of the 85 who test positive. Lee et al. measured 6.9% directly across 458,175 screens. Here is how to read that number.

### High sensitivity, low PPV

Mammography is a wide, fine-meshed safety net. Its job is to minimize missed cancers, and the price is false alarms.

- **Sensitivity is high (75–90%).** Of 100 women with undetected breast cancer, the test flags 75 to 90. The accepted floor for a radiologist is 75%; the U.S. average is 87%.
- **PPV₁ is low (3–8%).** Of 100 women flagged for a second look, only 3 to 8 have cancer. The rest are cysts, dense tissue, and harmless calcifications that a cautious reader flags rather than risk missing something.

Both ranges are the American College of Radiology's acceptable-performance bands (Carney et al.); a radiologist outside them is considered for additional training.

### The role of the base rate

The PPV is set less by the test than by how rare the condition is. Only 6 or 7 of every 1,000 women screened have breast cancer. A radiologist who recalls 83 of them to be sure of catching those 6 lands at a PPV₁ of about 7% no matter how carefully each image is read: the other 77 recalls are the 8% false-positive rate applied to 993 healthy women.

### How the detection process works

A positive screen is the start of a process, not a diagnosis. Each stage below is a round of the retesting picture above: the PPV coming out of one stage is the prevalence going into the next.

::: {.ppv-flow}
::: {.ppv-flow-step}
[Screening mammogram]{.ppv-flow-label}
flags about 8% of women for a closer look (recall)
:::
::: {.ppv-flow-step}
[Diagnostic imaging]{.ppv-flow-label}
additional views, ultrasound or MRI clear about four in five of those recalled
:::
::: {.ppv-flow-step}
[Biopsy]{.ppv-flow-label}
confirms cancer in 20–40% of the remaining cases (PPV₂)
:::
:::

In Lee et al.'s data, per 1,000 women screened: 83 are recalled, about 18 are recommended for biopsy, and 6 have cancer (5.8 found, 0.8 missed). PPV₁ is 6.9% at the first stage and PPV₂ is 32% at biopsy. A negative screen, by contrast, is very reassuring: NPV is about 99.9%. The earlier 2D digital mammography benchmark (Lehman et al., 2017) had the same sensitivity but lower specificity (89%), so it recalled 116 per 1,000 for a PPV₁ of 4.4% — the same lesson, with a noisier test.
